cases.title: Bharatpur–Bardaghat Power Line: Towers in Dumkibas Yards
cases.place: Dumkibas, Binayi Triveni Rural Municipality Ward No. 2, Nawalpur, Nepal
cases.point: Dumkibas, Binayi Triveni Rural Municipality, where the line's last towers were contested (approximate)

lenders.name: World Bank (IDA)
lenders.role: The Nepal-India Electricity Transmission and Trade Project, approved on 21 June 2011 for US$99 million, with US$39 million additional financing approved on 24 June 2013, financed the 74-kilometre Bharatpur–Bardaghat transmission line (Inspection Panel).

cases.conditions: IDA credit and grant financed construction of the Bharatpur–Bardaghat line, implemented by the Nepal Electricity Authority (NEA). The project closed on 31 October 2021 with the Dumkibas section unfinished; the Bank agreed a post-closure action plan with NEA to finish the resettlement plan (Inspection Panel).
cases.community: Residents said the line was rerouted through their crowded village without consultation, affecting 96 households (Request, as summarised by the Inspection Panel). Bank Management counted 46 landowners affected, 16 households that would have to move, and 5 losing land for tower pads; no one may live in the 30-metre right of way and trees over 4.5 metres are barred. On its January 2022 visit the Panel saw a tower already built in the backyard of a house where a poor, multi-generation Dalit family of eight lives, and heard from a homeowner that a tower was built on his land in the presence of police without notice or consent. Residents said banks would not accept land under the line as loan collateral (Inspection Panel; Kathmandu Post).
cases.suppression: In April 2021 residents protested the digging of a tower pad, which they said broke a Supreme Court stay order. They said armed police used tear gas and beat people; women told the Panel of knee and arm injuries that had not healed. Management said NEA and police reported protesters threw stones and injured NEA staff, and that both sides claim injuries (Inspection Panel).
cases.killed_note: No deaths reported in the sources used.
cases.outcome: The Supreme Court halted work on the last two towers in April 2021 and lifted the order on 27 June 2022 (Kathmandu Post). The Panel recommended an investigation on 16 February 2022 and the Board approved it on 3 March 2022. The parties chose mediation and on 11 April 2023 NEA and 63 residents signed a confidential agreement; by 2024, 65 payments had been made (43 for right-of-way land, 17 for structures, 5 for tower pads), fences were built around towers, and training and a community centre were funded. Nine requesters from one family left the process and did not sign (Dispute Resolution Service).

cases.confidence_note: The April 2021 clash is disputed: residents describe police violence, while NEA and police say protesters attacked first and both sides were hurt; no Bank staff saw it. Management said NEA had built towers only on public land in Dumkibas, which the homeowner's account contradicts. The settlement terms are confidential.

cases.ecosystem: Two towers were placed on the riverbank and two in forest without residents' consent, according to the Request; Management said the route chosen cleared the least forest and 25 trees are to be planted for each tree cut (Inspection Panel).

lvwhy.project: An IDA-financed high-voltage line was built through a crowded village, with police present for tower works.
lvwhy.land: Land under towers and a 30-metre corridor was taken or restricted; Management counted 16 households that would have to move.

cases.title: Cusco Via Expresa: Brickmakers Cleared from the Road Reserve
cases.place: Via Expresa Avenue, San Sebastián district, Cusco, Peru
cases.point: Via Expresa Avenue near Quispiquilla, San Sebastián district, where the land in the request lies (approximate)

lenders.name: World Bank (IBRD)
lenders.role: US$120 million loan for the Cusco Transport Improvement Project, approved on 28 February 2014; US$112.7 million of it for upgrading the Via Expresa Avenue (Inspection Panel).

cases.conditions: The loan financed widening of the Via Expresa; its Resettlement Action Plan named 18 informal users of the road reserve (10 brickmakers and 8 car washers) as entitled to training and six months' minimum wage, with a November 2016 cut-off date (Inspection Panel).
cases.community: On 2 September 2019 heavy machinery and police cleared brickmakers from the Via Expresa road reserve. Nine brickmakers who rented plots there joined the complaint. Three told the Panel they were woken around 5 a.m. and told to leave at once, that their small clay houses were destroyed and their bricks and materials taken, and that some were left without work and some homeless. The Panel reviewed their videos and photos: they show construction vehicles destroying and removing bricks with police nearby, piles of bricks and small structures being destroyed and removed, and police telling a man to leave a small structure before its demolition. The Panel noted a potential livelihood impact on poor and vulnerable people (Inspection Panel).
cases.suppression: The clearance was carried out with police present, together with Cusco's prosecutor's office and the municipal attorney's office (Inspection Panel, citing Management).
cases.killed_note: No deaths reported in the sources used.
cases.outcome: The Panel recommended no investigation in December 2020: land ownership was for Peru's courts and the brickmakers had not first gone to Bank Management, which committed to ask the borrower to review their eligibility. The Board agreed on 12 January 2021. Management said the 10 brickmakers listed in the plan had accepted assistance (Inspection Panel).

sources.title: Inspection Panel Report and Recommendation: Peru Cusco Transport Improvement Project

cases.confidence_note: Management says the 2 September 2019 action was a code enforcement action that used no force, involved no structures and followed at least three weeks' notice, though it agrees brickmakers and their materials were removed from the project area that day. It says evictions that destroyed houses elsewhere in Cusco were not linked to the project. The Panel made no finding of harm: it did not recommend an investigation because Management had not been told of the brickmakers' claims first. It is unclear whether the nine brickmakers who complained are among the 10 listed in the plan. Only the Panel's report documents the event.

lvwhy.project: Bank-financed widening of the Via Expresa required clearing its road reserve.
lvwhy.land: Brickmakers who rented plots in the road reserve lost their workplace and bricks when it was cleared for the works.

Dropped (third time). No credible source documents harm that actually happened to people or nature near Medupi after the 2010 IBRD loan. The death and asthma figures are modelled estimates. Residents' accounts come from a Fair Finance Coalition report whose authors say they did not test any causal link to Medupi (Daily Maverick, 2023). The 2017 Sunday Times report on Marapong centres on the older Matimba plant. The 2023 SAHRC action was a probe of a complaint, not a finding. Eskom's own Marapong monitoring (May 2024) recorded no exceedances of national air limits. The Inspection Panel found no current harm in 2011. Police dispersal of striking construction workers (2015) and a shooting of two workers by an unknown gunman were labour incidents not caused by the plant or forces acting for it. Complaint link ip:65 dropped with it.

Dropped: Bank role and timing do not match the harm. The harms in the Panel's 2007 report (a logging company cutting Batwa medicinal and caterpillar trees and destroying fields and sacred sites; villages and fields inside concessions without compensation; entry fees; promised schools and clinics missing) were caused by concession holders, most with titles from before the Bank's 2003 and 2005 operations. The Bank did not finance or require logging: its forest conditions were extending the 2002 moratorium on new concessions and starting a legal review meant to cancel illegal titles. The Panel said only that the review 'may have inadvertently' encouraged swaps and faster logging, on 'anecdotal information', and that the Batwa claims 'could not be properly assessed'. Its compliance findings were about procedure (no environmental assessment, Pygmies not identified). No source documents harm from the concessions the review later confirmed (2009). Complaint link ip:37 dropped with it.
